messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error of the mean (under H₀)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}
     = \frac{1.4}{6.3249}
     \approx 0.221
\]

So the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean (the “standard error”) is about **0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" but they provide sample mean, standard deviation, sample size, and population mean. They likely want the standard error or the standard deviation of the sampling distribution? The phrase "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" might refer to the standard error of the mean under H0: sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample std dev. Usually use sample std dev as estimate of sigma. So standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40)=6.3249. 1.4/6.3249=0.2213 approx. That is the standard error. Alternatively, if they want the standard deviation of the null distribution (i.e., difference between sample mean and population mean?), maybe they'd want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean under H0: sigma/sqrt(n). So answer ~0.221.

But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." Might be ambiguous. They might want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic under H0 is sqrt((n-1)/(n-2))? Actually t-distribution has variance n/(n-2) for df>2. But that's not typical. They probably just want the standard error.

Thus answer: standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.221. Provide explanation.
